exam3.question: If new research shows that the minimum velocity criteria used to diagnose >60% renal artery stenosis is actually 225cm/s, not 180cm/s, how will this affect the accuracy of the renal Doppler exam?

options.text: decrease will vary with patient population
no effect on the accuracy, only affects positive and negative predictive value
increase will vary with patient population

exam3.explanation: Negative predictive value refers to the ability of an exam to correctly predict the absence of disease. Raising the peak velocity required to identify a significant renal stenosis will decrease the negative predictive value. This occurs due to the increased amount of patients that have a lower velocity but truly demonstrate >60% stenosis in the renal artery. The positive predictive value will increase for the renal Doppler exam because more patients will actually have significant stenosis when their exam produces velocities above 225cm/s. Accuracy will increase because of the increase in truly positive exams compared to the total number of exams. The more people correctly diagnosed as positive, the greater the accuracy of an exam.

exam3.question: Hypothenar hammer syndrome and thoracic outlet syndrome are what type of vascular disorder?
exam3.explanation: TOS involves compression of the vessels in the thoracic outlet. Hypothenar hammer syndrome involves compression of the ulnar artery. Median arcuate ligament syndrome involves compression of the celiac artery or celiac trunk. There are many types that can be caused by tumors or congenital mal-positioning of vessels.

exam3.question: Which of the following is an absolute contraindication to an endovenous ablation?
exam3.explanation: An absolute contraindication is a situation which makes a particular treatment or procedure absolutely inadvisable. These include a known allergy to the injected material (ablation, steroid injection) , lack of appropriate equipment or skill to complete the procedure, uncooperative patient (uncontrolled movement during the procedure can result in injury, laceration or hemorrhage ) A relative contraindication is a condition which makes a particular treatment or procedure possibly inadvisable. Changes can be made to make the procedure safer or easier to perform. These include coagulopathy and the use of blood thinners, aspirin or antibiotics. if permitted by their physician, the patient can discontinue their blood thinner medication until their PT and INR values return to normal levels and then proceed with the invasive procedure. Warfarin, Coumadin, Jantoven, Xarelto, Pradaxa or Lovenox, Aspirin, Ibuprofen, NSAIDs should be stopped at least 7 days before a procedure and resumed 7 days after the procedure. Other relative contraindications include: Unsafe access route - must avoid large arteries and adjacent nerves Local infection, rash, or skin breakdown

exam3.question: Increased pressure in the venous system results in:
exam3.explanation: Increased pressure in the venous system results in edema as fluid is forced outward into surrounding tissues.

exam3.question: Which of the following is important information to record on the final report for a carotid Doppler exam on a patient with 50-69% ICA stenosis?

options.text: Transducer frequency used for the exam
Doppler angles used on the exam
Recommendation for TCD exam for associated intracerebral disease

exam3.explanation: A patient with 50-69% stenosis will be followed with serial ultrasound examinations annually or semiannually. The Doppler angles used in this exam should be duplicated on the serial exams for the most accurate assessment of changes in the level of stenosis.

exam3.question: Which of the following are collagen disorders that have increased risk for arterial dissection?

options.text: Paget Schroetter syndrome and Raynaud syndrome
Shone complex and Blue Toe syndrome

exam3.explanation: Marfan syndrome and Ehler-Danlos syndrome are collagen disorders that can lead to the formation of arterial aneurysm or dissection. Shone complex is a group of cardiac defects and defects of the aortic arch and valve. Blue Toe syndrome is caused by emboli from an AAA with mural thrombus, Paget Schroetter syndrome affects the upper extremity veins. Raynaud syndrome is a collagen disorder that reduces flow to the hands/feet. Polycythemia vera is a rare cancer that causes blood thickening,

exam3.question: Anticoagulant therapy is a contraindication for:
exam3.explanation: Anticoagulant therapy is a contraindication for pseudoaneurysm treatment. The goal of compression therapy and thrombin injection is to promote thrombus formation. Anticoagulant therapy works to reduce thrombus formation.

exam3.question: A patient presents for a 3-month follow-up on his aortic endograft. The aortic sac has increased in size by 0.8cm since the last ultrasound evaluation performed 2 months ago. No endoleak was detected on ultrasound or CT evaluation. What is the most likely cause for the diameter change?
exam3.explanation: Endotension- no leak present but there is continued expansion of the aneurysm sac greater than 5 mm; sometimes referred to as Type V Endoleak

exam3.question: Which of the following is a contraindication for harvesting of the great saphenous vein?

options.text: chronic obstruction of the femoral vein
valvular incompetence in the great saphenous vein
chronic obstruction of the peroneal veins
Baker's cyst in the ipsilateral popliteal fossa

exam3.explanation: IT IS VERY IMPORTANT to evaluate the venous outflow system of a patient prior to removal or closure of the saphenous vein. If the deep system is obstructed and the superficial system is the main outflow for the leg, the saphenous vein cannot be removed/closed.

exam3.question: A patient presents with gangrene of the foot and toes. The most likely cause of these symptoms i

options.text: chronic occlusion of the popliteal artery
a Scm aortic aneurysm with mural thrombus
: extensive deep and superficial vein thrombosis.

exam3.explanation: Venous gangrene usually involves the foot and all toes, while arterial gangrene usually involves one or two toes.

exam3.question: The most common cause of hemodialysis graft failure is
exam3.explanation: The most common cause of hemodialysis graft failure is thrombus formation.

exam3.question: Which of the following causes flow reversal in venous perforators?

options.text: combination of superficial and deep thrombosis,

normally bidirectional to help equalize pressures in the deep and superficial systems

exam3.explanation: Abnormal results for a penile Doppler evaluation that suggest impotence include <30cm/s peak systolic flow velocity and a peak pressure <60mmHg.

exam3.question: Which of the following is a limitation of the 2D evaluation of the extremity veins?

options.text: increased amount of fibrous tissues and ligaments in the adductor canal
patient cannot lay flat for exam
inability to visualize the vessels immediately posterior to the inguinal ligament

exam3.explanation: Limitations of venous duplex evaluations: * Non-visualization of veins due to excessive transducer pressure * Location of the subclavian vein beneath the clavicle * increased amount of fibrous tissues and ligaments in the adductor canal Patient that cannot be semi-erect or standing for exam The inguinal ligament is not normally visible on ultrasound evaluation, and it does not cause non-visualization of adjacent anatomy. The adductor canal contains several ligaments and connective tissues that limit compression of the distal femoral vein. Increased transducer pressure can cause non-visualization of normal veins. The subclavian vein courses posterior to the clavicle, which limits manual compression. The superficial venous systems of the upper and lower extremities can be easily compressed causing non-visualization Patients for DVT exams should be scanned in the semierect position to dilate the veins for easier visualization. A supine patient can cause the veins to be difficult to identity. Insufficiency exams should be performed with the patient standing, to engorge the veins with blood and encourage the display of reflux. A supine patient could cause false negative results for reflux.

exam3.question: When evaluating the left arm for potential placement of a central venous catheter, you identify multiple small venous collaterals surrounding the subclavian vein. What should you do next?

options.text: evaluate the extremity arteries instead for potential catheterization
measure the largest collateral for potential pathway for the catheter
evaluate the venous system in the right arm
tell the physician the patient is not a candidate for catheter placement

exam3.explanation: If venous collaterals are identified on the pre-procedure scan for central venous catheter placement, there is a stenosis or occlusion of the adjacent major vein. The patency and size of the collaterals are insignificant when deciding not to use that extremity for the catheter. The mere presence of the collaterals indicates an issue with that venous pathway. Normal veins are preferred for catheter placement. These findings are usually going to change the access point or placement of the central venous catheter to another vein/arm, but the Sonographer does not advise the physician on that decision. The opposite arm should be evaluated for an alternate location for catheter placement. Arteries cannot be used for the same purpose as veins for catheter delivery of medications,

exam3.question: The TIPS procedure is performed to correct what condition?
exam3.explanation: A transjugular intrahepatic porto-systemic shunt is used to bypass the liver and relieve portal HTN. The portal system is directly connected to the IJV or Hepatic veins. TIPS - Portal HTN Relief

exam3.question: Which of the following is NOT normally a part of a test for vasculogenic impotence?

options.text: Obtain blood pressures in the arms and ankles
Measure the length of the cavernous arteries
Obtain Doppler samples of the CFA, PTA and DPA
Obtain Doppler samples of the cavernous arteries and veins in the penis

exam3.explanation: When performing a penile Doppler exam, obtain Doppler samples of the CFA, cavernous arteries and veins in the penis. Doppler samples will also be taken in the PTA and DPA while performing ankle pressures. The ABI should be evaluated to determine if PAD can be causing the erectile dysfunction. The diameter of the cavernous arteries should be measured.

exam3.question: Which of the following terms would be used to describe abnormal venous flow in the deep veins of the thigh?
exam3.explanation: The term pulsatilty refers to repetitive flow changes demonstrated on the Doppler tracing. Veins closest to the heart will demonstrate cardiac pulsatility due to the changes in right atrial pressure. It can be equated to a "ripple effect’, like a stone being thrown into a pool of water. The variations in flow are demonstrated in vessels further from the heart as they become engorged with blood. If venous flow is pulsatile in the lower extremities, cardiac complications like CHF or severe tricuspid regurgitation should be suspected. Normal venous flow varies with respiration and has very low velocity. exam3.question: A patient presents for a venous insufficiency exam but is unable to stand for the exam. How will this affect your exam?

options.text: Venous reflux may not be demonstrated in veins where it is actually present.
The PPG tracings will be increased in amplitude.
No change as long as they can move their feet to perform the heel raises.
The segmental pressures will be falsely elevated.

exam3.explanation: Standing increases hydrostatic pressure to better demonstrate the reflux. If the patient is supine, a false negative exam could be obtained because the augmentation response will be diminished without hydrostatic pressure. A seated patient will have bent knees and hip joints which can inhibit/reduce the flow response to augmentation.

exam3.question: A diabetic patient presents for a segmental pressure exam. The calf and ankle vessels are non-compressible with up to 220mmHg. What alternative exam can be performed to evaluate lower extremity pressures?
exam3.explanation: The tiny vessels of the toes are usually spared from medial calcification. PPG waveforms and pressure measurements can be taken on the toes when the ankle pressures are falsely elevated.

exam3.question: Which blood vessel is most commonly evaluated with Doppler to obtain the thigh pressure when performing a segmental pressure exam?

options.text: distal calf artery with lowest ankle pressure
distal calf artery with highest ankle pressure
popliteal artery just above the calf cuff
femoral artery just proximal to the thigh cuff

exam3.explanation: The PTA or DPA that yields the highest pressure at the ankle should be used to obtain the pressures for the remaining arterial segments. The Doppier signal from the calf arteries are used for ALL pressure measurements in the leg.

exam3.question: Which of the following carries an increased risk of developing varicose veins?

options.text: Sitting with legs elevated for long periods of time
Wearing flat shoes instead of high heels

exam3.explanation: Oral contraceptive use will increase the risk of developing varicose veins. Family history, pregnancy and obesity also increase the risk. The other three choices would reduce the risk of developing varicose veins.

exam3.question: Which of the following is used to determine the capability of healing a wound or identify a site for amputation?
exam3.explanation: Transcutaneous oximetry evaluates oxygen supply and consumption in the tissues surrounding a wound. The partial pressure of the oxygen is recorded in the tissues around the wound. 70-80mmHg indicates normal pressure, <4Ommbg indicates tissue hypoxia. The information is used to determine the healing ability of the wound.

exam3.question: According to the Appropriate Use Criteria, which of the following is an appropriate indication for an lower extremity venous duplex exam for venous insufficiency?
exam3.explanation: Hyperpigmentation of the distal calf occurs with chronic venous insufficiency. The waste products in the venous blood that pools in the calf cannot be absorbed by osmosis. Telangiectasia refers to dilated veins that appear as spider veins on the legs. This appearance has not been associated with insufficiency in the larger superficial veins.

occurs in patients with an obstructed vascular system

exam3.question: If the acceleration time is >140ms in both common femoral arteries:

options.text: bilateral internal iliac disease is suspected
unilateral external iliac disease is suspected

exam3.explanation: If the acceleration time is >140ms in both common femoral arteries, aortic disease is suspected. Increased or longer AT indicates a proximal obstruction. If the acceleration time is >140ms in one common femoral artery, ipsilateral iliac stenosis is suspected. Decreased or shorter AT indicates a distal obstruction.

exam3.question: Which of the following vessels typically supplies blood to a carotid body tumor?

options.text: branches of the internal carotid artery
branches of the external carotid artery
branches of the middle cerebral artery

exam3.explanation: Branches of the ECA typically supply blood to a carotid body tumor. Because the ICA has no extracranial branches, it is much less commonly the source of arterial flow to a carotid body tumor.

exam3.question: While scanning the popliteal artery, you notice a thrombus in the popliteal vein. Which vein(s) should be evaluated next for ascending propagation of the clot?
exam3.explanation: If a clot is identified in the popliteal vein, the distal femoral vein should be evaluated next for propagation of the thrombus.

exam3.question: The preferred imaging plane to measure the AP dimension of the aorta is:
exam3.explanation: The sagittal plane is the preferred imaging plane to measure the AP dimension of the aorta.

exam3.question: Which of the following is not proper procedure for a venous PPG evaluation of the legs?

options.text: Always place the sensor over the largest varicose vein in the calf
A tourniquet is applied to the leg after initial testing shows a VRT < 20 sec
Patient is seated with legs dangling over edge of bed for the exam
The optimal speed for the strip chart recorder is Smm/sec

Never place the PPG sensor on an open wound, ulcer or varicose vein. A strip chart recorder documents flow changes. The optimal speed for the strip chart recorder is Smm/sec. The sample size will only affect the amount of flow sampled and is not useful for determining the vessel being evaluated.

exam3.question: A patient presents with splenomegaly and multiple, small, tortuous vessels are visualized in the porta hepatis area of the liver. These vessels most likely represent:
exam3.explanation: Cavernous transformation of the vessels at the porta hepatis refers to the formation of varices from the increased portal pressure with portal HTN. Accessory veins dilate at the porta hepatis due to the backlog of blood flow. These vessels are small and tortuous. Splenomegaly is another sign of portal HTN and a backlog in the blood flow in the portal system.

exam3.question: Where do the plantar arteries originate?

options.text: from the anterior tibial artery posterior to the medial malleolus
from the peroneal artery just past the Achilles tendon attachment at the heel
from the anterior tibial artery anterior to the medial malleolus
from the posterior tibial artery posterior to the medial malleolus

exam3.explanation: The plantar arteries originate from the PTA posterior to the medial malleolus.

exam3.question: The posterior communicating artery connects the:

options.text: right and left sides of the circle of willis

exam3.explanation: The posterior communicators connect the posterior cerebral circulation to the anterior cerebral circulation (PCA and the MCA). The ACA and MCA are part of the anterior circulation. The PCA and basilar/vertebral arteries are part of the posterior circulation.

exam3.question: You obtain the PPG tracing from the second digit of the left hand. Which of the following is NOT an expected cause for the findings?
exam3.explanation: Leriche syndrome refers to stenosis or occlusion of the distal aorta. This would lead to a similar PPG tracing from the LOWER extremity digits.

exam3.question: You are performing a carotid duplex on a patient that had a carotid endarterectomy 2 weeks ago. There is homogeneous material lining the ICA and bulb and Doppler demonstrates turbulence and elevated velocities. Which of the following is the most likely cause for these findings?

options.text: residual blockage from suboptimal surgical techniques

exam3.explanation: Within the first month post-op, restenosis is attributed to suboptimal surgical techniques. Narrowing over the first 24 months after CEA is attributed to neointimal hyperplasia. After 2 years, stenosis occurs due to progression of atherosclerotic disease.

exam3.question: Which of the following is NOT an appropriate reason to terminate the treadmill exercise for a lower extremity arterial exam?

options.text: patient complains that the treadmill is too noisy
patient complains of shortness of breath

exam3.explanation: Anytime the patient reports symptoms of pain in the legs or the chest, the exam should be terminated. Never try to talk the patient into continuing the exam. Always record the duration of the exercise, location of the symptoms and changes in ankle pressures,

exam3.question: When performing serial exams on an in situ venous bypass graft, indicates significant graft failure.

options.text: conversion of the waveform from triphasic to biphasic
a decrease in peak systolic velocity of 30cm/s from the last exam
a decrease in ABI of 0.10 from the last exam
an increase in end diastolic velocity greater than 30cm/s from the last exam

exam3.explanation: Serial exams that demonstrate a decrease in the PSV or 30cm/s or more and/or a decrease in the ABI of 0.15 or more indicate poor performance of the graft on the current exam.

exam3.question: Which cardiac abnormality usually has NO effect on the peak systolic velocities in the carotid arteries?
exam3.explanation: Cardiac structure and function should be considered in all vascular evaluations. Changes in cardiac function can affect the velocities in the arterial system and change the flow characteristics of the venous system. Mitral regurgitation does NOT affect, the systolic velocities in the arterial system. Aortic stenosis, mitral stenosis, CHF, diastolic dysfunction, dilated cardiomyopathy and CAD can reduce the cardiac ejection fraction and falsely reduce the PSV in the arterial system. Systemic HTN, aortic regurgitation, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and compensatory heart beats with arrhythmias can falsely elevate the PSV.
